```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  echo = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 150,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
library(knowledge)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
# pkgdown sets IN_PKGDOWN while it builds the website: the site gets the interactive map, the package copy the
# static one
on_site <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
```

```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_chinook.R
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("chinook_rearing.rds"))
seg <- readRDS(vd("bulk_segments.rds"))
water <- readRDS(vd("bulk_water.rds"))

tune <- x$tune
summ <- x$summary
meta <- x$meta
cmp <- x$compare
dflt <- tune[tune$is_default, ]
rec <- tune[tune$recommended %in% TRUE, ]
region <- tune[tune$in_region, ]
all_row <- cmp[cmp$watershed_group_code == "ALL", ]
per_group <- cmp[cmp$watershed_group_code != "ALL", ]
map_row <- cmp[cmp$watershed_group_code == meta$map_group, ]
seeds <- x$seeds
honest <- x$honest
ge <- x$grad_ext
ge_best <- ge[ge$ddev_best == 0, ]
ge_reg <- ge$grad_max[ge$in_region > 0]

# formatting
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
n1 <- function(v) format(round(v, 1), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 1, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
pc <- function(v, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * v, format = "f", digits = d), " %")
grad <- function(g) paste0(signif(100 * g, 4), " %")
km_d <- function(d) if (d >= 1000) paste(format(d / 1000, trim = TRUE), "km") else paste(d, "m")
lst <- function(v, and = "and") if (length(v) < 2) v else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), and, v[length(v)])
words <- function(r) {
  size <- if (r$size_var == "mad") sprintf("an average flow of at least %s m³/s", format(r$size_min, trim = TRUE))
          else sprintf("a channel at least %s m wide", format(r$size_min, trim = TRUE))
  if (is.na(r$exc_q)) return(sprintf("a slope of at most %s, and %s", grad(r$grad_max), size))
  sprintf("a slope of at most %s, and either %s or a river of at least %s m³/s within %s downstream",
          grad(r$grad_max), size, r$exc_q, km_d(r$exc_d))
}
# every rule in the close-call set has the same shape; the sentences below say so
stopifnot(all(region$size_var == "mad"), all(!is.na(region$exc_q)), dflt$ddev_best > dflt$se_diff,
          all(region$departures == 3))

# the stricter bar: the same choice from rules within 1.96 standard errors
tune$in_196 <- tune$converged %in% TRUE & tune$ddev_best <= 1.96 * tune$se_diff
ch196 <- knw_tune_repick(tune, se_mult = 1.96)
# at 1.96 the flow floor holds, the slope goes back to link's, the near-a-river allowance goes, and link's rule
# stays out
stopifnot(ch196$size_var == "mad", ch196$size_min == rec$size_min, ch196$grad_max == dflt$grad_max, is.na(ch196$exc_q),
          ch196$rule != dflt$rule, !tune$in_196[tune$is_default], sum(tune$in_196) == ch196$n_region,
          all(tune$in_196[tune$in_region]))

# steeper slope limits (scored later on a longer list, up to 30 %)
stopifnot(nrow(ge_best) == 1, ge_best$grad_max > rec$grad_max, all(ge$in_region[ge$grad_max >= min(ge_reg)] > 0))

boot_mad <- sum(tune$boot_rec_share[tune$size_var == "mad"])
boot_grad <- sum(tune$boot_rec_share[tune$grad_max == rec$grad_max])
stopifnot(boot_mad > 0.9, boot_grad < 0.5)

wl <- x$wetland
stopifnot(abs(wl$km_tuned - 10200) < 200, wl$grade_median_tuned < 0.05)

link_site <- "https://www.newgraphenvironment.com/link/"
link_default <- sprintf("https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/link/tree/%s/inst/extdata/configs/default", meta$link_sha)
```

New Graph Environment maps where fish can live in British Columbia's streams with
[`link`](`r link_site`) [@irvine2026linkDevelop], an R package that marks every stream segment as spawning or
rearing habitat for each species, and as reachable by fish or not. Its standard settings, called
[`default`](`r link_default`), start from those [bcfishpass](https://smnorris.github.io/bcfishpass/) has used for years
[@norris2024smnorrisbcfishpass]. This article tests one of them, where young chinook salmon rear, against the
province's electrofishing records.

**The answer.** The records support a different rule from link's current one: **`r words(rec)`**. link now asks
for `r words(dflt)`. The new rule draws `r n1(-all_row$change_pct)` % less habitat across the province, and
chinook are caught far more often inside it than outside. Its cut-offs are a judgment call, though: under a stricter
bar only the flow floor holds (below).

## What does link do now?

link counts a stream segment as chinook rearing habitat when chinook can reach it, its slope is at most
`r grad(dflt$grad_max)`, and its channel is at least `r dflt$size_min` m wide. link can size streams by width or by
flow, set group by group. Its `default` uses width in every group, and every comparison here is against that. link's
own flow cut-offs were scored as candidates, not used as the starting point. Rivers, wetlands and lakes have their own
conditions (last section).

## What records were used?

The province's stream atlas divides British Columbia into **watershed groups**, large basins such as the Bulkley.
The records are the Fisheries Data Information System's electrofishing sites [@provinceofbritishcolumbia2022FisheriesData]: where crews fished, and
whether they caught chinook. Each site was matched to the records it produced in bcfishobs [@norris2024smnorrisbcfishobs] and placed on link's
streams, built on the BC Freshwater Atlas through fwapg [@norris2024smnorrisfwapg], with flows from wet [@irvine2026wetStream]
and the rules run by fresh [@irvine2026freshFreshwater]. Sites
were kept when they were on ordinary stream lines, of a usual fished area, with no barrier to chinook downstream, in a
group where link expects chinook: `r n0(summ$visits_in)` sites in `r summ$groups` groups. The tests use the
`r summ$groups_both` groups where chinook were caught at some sites and not others:
**`r n0(dflt$n_visits)` sites, `r n0(dflt$n_detect)` with chinook**.

## How were rules compared?

Each candidate rule sets three dials:

- **the smallest stream**: an average flow of `r lst(sort(unique(tune$size_min[tune$size_var == "mad"])), "or")` m³/s,
  or a channel width of `r lst(sort(unique(tune$size_min[tune$size_var == "width"])), "or")` m;
- **the steepest slope**: `r lst(grad(sort(unique(tune$grad_max))), "or")`;
- **a near-a-river allowance**: none, or a stream below the smallest size still counts when a river of
  `r lst(sort(unique(na.omit(tune$exc_q))), "or")` m³/s is within
  `r lst(format(sort(unique(na.omit(tune$exc_d))), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "or")` m downstream.

That makes `r n0(nrow(tune))` rules, link's among them. Each was scored on watersheds it never saw: the groups were
split into `r meta$spec$folds` sets, and each set was predicted by a model fitted to the other four. The score adds up
how far each prediction was from what the crew found; lower is better.

## Which rule fits best, and how sure are we?

**Close-call rules.** Scores carry error: another draw of watersheds would rank close rules differently. So the tuning
kept every rule within one standard error of the best. That rule of thumb began with pruning classification trees
[@breiman_etal1984ClassificationRegression; as cited in @chen_yang2021OneStandard] and is now a common way to prefer
the simpler of close models [@hastie_etal2009ElementsStatistical]. It is a convention fixed before the run, not a line
below which rules are equal. There is no evidence it consistently beats taking the best score, though it often picks
fewer variables [@chen_yang2021OneStandard]. The error it rests on has no unbiased estimate
[@bengio_grandvalet2004NoUnbiased], and the usual estimate is often too small
[@bengio_grandvalet2004NoUnbiased; @bates_etal2024CrossValidationWhat], though it can also be too large
[@chen_yang2021OneStandard]. For chinook, `r nrow(region)` rules are close calls,
all with a flow floor of `r min(region$size_min)` to `r max(region$size_min)` m³/s, the near-a-river allowance, and a
slope limit of `r lst(grad(sort(unique(region$grad_max))), "or")`. From them, the rule fixed in advance takes the one
closest to link's; all differ in every dial, so it is the best scorer. link's rule is
`r n1(dflt$ddev_best / dflt$se_diff)` standard errors behind it. It calls fewer sites habitat
(`r n0(rec$n_in)` against `r n0(dflt$n_in)`) and catches as many chinook there (`r n0(rec$n_detect_in)` against
`r n0(dflt$n_detect_in)`).

```{r profile, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "How close the best rule using each value of each dial comes to the best rule overall, as score above the best (lower is better). Dark blue: at least one rule with that value is a close call at one standard error; light blue: only at 1.96 standard errors; white: neither. The orange ring marks link's current value."}
dial <- function(lab, v, key) {
  tune |>
    mutate(value = v) |>
    group_by(value, key = key) |>
    summarise(best = min(ddev_best), one = any(in_region), strict = any(in_196), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(part = lab)
}
size_lab <- paste(ifelse(tune$size_var == "mad", "flow", "width"), as.character(tune$size_min))
size_key <- ifelse(tune$size_var == "mad", tune$size_min, 10 + tune$size_min)
prof <- bind_rows(
  dial("Smallest stream (flow m³/s or width m)", size_lab, size_key),
  dial("Steepest slope", grad(tune$grad_max), tune$grad_max),
  dial("Near-a-river allowance: river size (m³/s)", ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_q), "none", format(tune$exc_q, trim = TRUE)),
       ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_q), -1, tune$exc_q)),
  dial("Near-a-river allowance: distance (m)",
       ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_d), "none", format(tune$exc_d, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)),
       ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_d), -1, tune$exc_d))
)
prof$part <- factor(prof$part, levels = unique(prof$part))
prof <- prof |>
  group_by(part) |>
  mutate(value = factor(value, levels = unique(value[order(key)]))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(close = factor(ifelse(one, "close call at one SE", ifelse(strict, "only at 1.96 SE", "neither")),
                        levels = c("close call at one SE", "only at 1.96 SE", "neither")))
dflt_vals <- tibble::tibble(
  part = factor(levels(prof$part), levels = levels(prof$part)),
  value = c(paste("width", as.character(dflt$size_min)), grad(dflt$grad_max), "none", "none")
)
dpts <- inner_join(prof, dflt_vals, by = c("part", "value"))
stopifnot(nrow(dpts) == 4)
ggplot(prof, aes(value, best)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = close), shape = 21, size = 2.6, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_point(data = dpts, shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 1, colour = "#d95f02", fill = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("close call at one SE" = "#1b6ca8", "only at 1.96 SE" = "#9ecae1", "neither" = "white"),
                    drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~part, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Score above the best rule") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The flow floors near the best are close calls at one standard error and no width floor is; the slope limit is
flat from `r grad(min(region$grad_max))` up.

**A stricter bar.** Widen the close calls to 1.96 standard errors and `r n0(ch196$n_region)` rules are close calls
instead of `r nrow(region)`. The same choice then changes:

```{r strict}
cell <- function(r) {
  c(n0(r$n_region),
    if (r$size_var == "mad") paste(format(r$size_min, trim = TRUE), "m³/s average flow")
    else paste(format(r$size_min, trim = TRUE), "m channel width"),
    grad(r$grad_max),
    if (is.na(r$exc_q)) "none" else paste0("a ", r$exc_q, " m³/s river within ", km_d(r$exc_d)))
}
rec1 <- rec
rec1$n_region <- nrow(region)
tab <- data.frame(rbind(cell(rec1), cell(ch196), cell(transform(dflt, n_region = NA))))
tab[3, 1] <- "outside both"
tab <- cbind(c("Chosen at one standard error", "Chosen at 1.96", "link's current rule"), tab)
names(tab) <- c(" ", "Close-call rules", "Smallest stream", "Steepest slope", "Near-a-river allowance")
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrlll",
             caption = "The chinook rule chosen from the close calls at each bar, beside link's current rule.")
```

The flow floor holds, but the slope limit goes back to link's `r grad(dflt$grad_max)` and the near-a-river allowance
drops out. link's own rule is still not a close call. link's thresholds table gives the choice at 1.96 for every
species tuned (`rule_196`).

**Two other checks.** Split into sets again with `r nrow(seeds)` other random draws, the recommended rule is a close
call on `r sum(seeds$main_rec_in_region)` and link's on `r sum(seeds$default_in_region)`. Chosen on four sets and
scored on the fifth, the chosen rule beats link's on `r sum(honest$dev_rec < honest$dev_default)` of
`r nrow(honest)` and `r if (sum(honest$dev_rec) < sum(honest$dev_default)) "beats it" else "loses to it"` overall.
Redrawing the groups `r meta$spec$n_boot` times, a flow floor is chosen in
`r if (isTRUE(all.equal(boot_mad, 1))) "every draw" else paste(pc(boot_mad, 1), "of draws")` but the recommended slope limit in only
`r pc(boot_grad)`: the shape is steady, the slope limit is not.

## Why does a nearby river matter?

Young chinook move up from large rivers into small streams close by. A model fitted after the choice, with flow and
distance to a river of at least `r meta$curve_ref$q` m³/s together, gives the chance of a catch on one standard
visit:

```{r surface-tab}
sf_ <- x$surface
dists <- sort(unique(sf_$dist_m))
st <- data.frame(`Stream flow (m³/s)` = format(sort(unique(sf_$size)), trim = TRUE, drop0trailing = TRUE),
                 check.names = FALSE)
for (dm in dists) {
  col <- if (dm >= meta$curve_ref$dist_cap_m) paste(km_d(dm), "or more") else km_d(dm)
  st[[col]] <- pc(sf_$rate[sf_$dist_m == dm][order(sf_$size[sf_$dist_m == dm])], 1)
}
knitr::kable(st, align = paste0("l", strrep("r", length(dists))),
             caption = paste0("The fitted chance of catching chinook on one standard visit, by stream flow (rows) and by ",
                              "distance downstream to a river of at least ", meta$curve_ref$q, " m³/s (columns), at a ",
                              "slope of ", grad(meta$curve_ref$gradient), "."))
r_at <- function(s, dm) sf_$rate[sf_$size == s & sf_$dist_m == dm]
near <- sf_$rate[sf_$dist_m == min(dists)]
```

Within `r km_d(min(dists))` of a river the chance is about the same whatever the stream's flow,
`r pc(min(near), 1)` to `r pc(max(near), 1)`. Ten kilometres away it rises with flow, from
`r pc(r_at(min(sf_$size), 10000), 1)` to `r pc(r_at(max(sf_$size), 10000), 1)`. That is the shape the recommended
rule draws: beside a river a small stream counts, away from one only a larger stream does.

## What changes on the ground?

Both rules were run through all of link's steps on the `r nrow(per_group)` watershed groups link classifies for
chinook: `r n0(all_row$default_km)` km of rearing habitat under link's rule, `r n0(all_row$tuned_km)` km under the
recommended one. The change ranges from `r n1(min(per_group$change_pct))` % to `r n1(max(per_group$change_pct))` %
by group. In the Bulkley the recommended rule draws `r n0(map_row$tuned_km)` km against `r n0(map_row$default_km)`.
`r if (on_site) "On the map, click a stream for what each rule reads there; the switch at the top right shows the grade, the use to expect on each segment." else ""`

```{r map-static, eval = !on_site, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6.9, out.width = "80%", fig.cap = paste0("Chinook rearing in the Bulkley (", meta$map_group, ") under each rule: kept by both, lost (link's rule only) and gained (the legend's 'tuned only', the recommended rule only). Line width follows stream order.")}
f1 <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
knw_compare_map(seg, water, png = f1, panels = "rules")
grid::grid.raster(png::readPNG(f1))
```

```{r map-site, eval = on_site, out.width = "100%"}
knw_compare_mapgl(seg, water, title = "Habitat by rule", background = "esri_topo")
```

Orange is mostly the upper reaches of tributaries, where flow falls below the floor more than `r km_d(rec$exc_d)`
from a river. Green is short reaches of small streams beside a river. The rest of the change comes from the step that
keeps rearing only where it links to spawning, which keeps different stretches under each rule.

```{r checks}
fv <- x$checks[x$checks$check == "fdis_visits", ]
rate <- function(r, s) {
  v <- fv[fv$rule == r & fv$segment == s, ]
  v$n_detect / v$n
}
```

**A check.** On the `r n0(sum(fv$n[fv$rule == "default"]))` electrofishing sites on reachable streams in those
groups, chinook were caught at `r pc(rate("tuned", "rearing"))` of sites on the recommended rule's habitat and
`r pc(rate("tuned", "accessible_not_rearing"), 1)` elsewhere, against `r pc(rate("default", "rearing"))` and
`r pc(rate("default", "accessible_not_rearing"), 1)` for link's. These sites overlap the ones scored, so this shows the
rule does what it was chosen to do, not that it predicts new places.

## Before you use it

- **It is about young chinook in streams.** It was fitted to juvenile chinook caught by electrofishing in streams and
  says nothing about spawning. River polygons share the stream slope limit, so they get `r grad(rec$grad_max)` too,
  though no site in one was scored. A line drawn through a wetland of 1 ha or more passes link's wetland condition
  under both rules whatever its size, slope or distance from a river, and is rearing wherever it connects to spawning:
  about `r n0(round(wl$km_tuned, -2))` km of chinook rearing, with a median grade of
  `r formatC(wl$grade_median_tuned, format = "f", digits = 2)`. Lakes keep their own condition.
- **The cut-offs are a judgment call.** Chinook get gradually less common as streams get smaller and steeper; there is
  no flow or slope where they stop. At one standard error, flow floors of `r min(region$size_min)` to
  `r max(region$size_min)` m³/s fit almost as well; at 1.96, only the flow floor holds.
- **Steeper slopes fit nearly as well.** Scored again with slope limits up to `r grad(max(ge$grad_max))`, the same
  procedure picks `r grad(ge_best$grad_max)`, and every limit from `r grad(min(ge_reg))` to `r grad(max(ge_reg))` has
  close-call rules. `r grad(rec$grad_max)` is kept because every species is tuned on one shared list of limits.
- **On the map, distance is measured from the bottom of each segment.** To choose the rule, the distance to a river
  was measured from each site. On the map it is measured from each segment's downstream end, so when that end is within
  `r km_d(rec$exc_d)` of the river the whole segment counts.
